examples: Simply apologizing won't settle this serious mistake.
If someone leaked confidential information, a warning alone probably won't be enough.
Since we caused trouble for so many people, an explanation alone won't be enough.
Drunk driving is a social problem, and in some cases a fine alone isn't the end of it.
This scandal is a company-wide problem; an apology alone cannot settle it.
This is a matter of human life. It's no joking matter!
fields.explain:
Used when judging that the consequences/measures required must go beyond the level of "just …".
Often seen in legal, administrative, business and news contexts; serious nuance.
The one making the judgment can be the speaker or society/general norms.
Used with nouns for actions/measures:謝罪・注意・反省・説明・弁償・処分…

• Doing just … won't settle it; the problem cannot be overlooked or solved only by …; stricter measures/sanctions are needed.
• Implies seriousness, legal/social/moral responsibility; often used with "謝る・注意・弁償・説明" etc.
• Strong, normative judgment: "that is not enough/not acceptable".
• "～だけでは済まされない" is formal and objective; "～だけではすまない" is more neutral.
fields.notes:
• In kanji it is usually written 済む→済まない; both すまない／済まない are used.
• The implied subject is social norms: "by common sense/by the rules, it cannot be just…".
• In formal texts and the news, the passive variant "～済まされない" appears often.
mistakes: Confusing it with "～だけではない" (completely different meaning: listing, no judgment).
Using it with light, everyday content makes the sentence sound too heavy: × 宿題を忘れて、謝るだけではすまない (may be excessive in an ordinary student situation).
Dropping "だけ": × 謝るではすまない → it must be 謝るだけではすまない.

rows: Just … is not enough/won't settle it
<ruby>謝<rt>あやま</rt></ruby>るだけではすまない
Additional listing; no implication of punishment
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>だけではない、<ruby>英語<rt>えいご</rt></ruby>もできる
Implies "society/the law will not let it pass"
<ruby>処分<rt>しょぶん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>注意<rt>ちゅうい</rt></ruby>だけでは<ruby>済<rt>す</rt></ruby>まされない
Does not stop at the scope of …
Focuses on expanding the scope; not necessarily a sanction
<ruby>影響<rt>えいきょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>国内<rt>こくない</rt></ruby>にとどまらない

examples: He's always complaining, saying his pay is low, his boss is strict, and so on.
On my days off, what with cleaning and laundry, the day is over in no time.
Kids are crazy about things like video games and manga.
My younger sister keeps going on about how her room is small, how it's cold, and so on.
He talks about studying English, studying abroad and so on, but in the end he never does anything.
What with business trips and meetings, my schedule is packed this week.
fields.explain:
Usually used when the speaker wants to show annoyance, criticism or weariness; it can also be fairly neutral, but a mild negative nuance is common.
The listed phrase is often followed by と言う／と騒ぐ／として…／で…／して… to state the next action/evaluation.
It does not list everything; it gives only a few typical examples, implying "there are many more".
Do not use です/ます directly before だの. Use the plain form: N/na-adjective + だ; i-adjectives/verbs stay as they are.
Can be used with the past tense/aspect:行った だの 買った だの と言う（went, bought…）.
Formality: natural spoken language, suited to conversation, diaries and social media; be careful in formal documents.

• Meaning: Lists a few typical examples, "… and …, and so on", often with a nuance of annoyance, criticism, complaint, or a negative/bothersome evaluation. Non-exhaustive: these are only examples, not a complete list.
• Speaker's attitude: Usually shows mild to moderate negative emotion (annoyed, fed up, tired), or judges something as messy and confusing.
• Grammar: Attaches to the plain form. Nouns/na-adjectives need "だ". I-adjectives/verbs keep their plain form, then add "だの".
• Position: The phrase "AだのBだの" can come before the particle と to link to 言う/騒ぐ…, or before で/して to state a cause/manner.
• Formality: Leans toward spoken language; rarely used in formal written language, or requires care with style.
• Number: Usually 2 items; 3 or more are possible; the last item usually also takes "だの".
fields.notes:
• Grammatically, だの is a listing particle that follows the "plain form"; with N/na-adjectives, "だ" is part of the plain form, so it appears before "の".
• Style-switching tip: AだのBだの → AやBなど (reduces the critical nuance); or AとかBとか (neutral spoken language).
• "Aだの何だの" means "A and all sorts of other stuff", emphasizing "there are many other things not worth listing".
• In quoted speech you may see: 「…」だの「…」だのと言う（quoting word for word to emphasize that the person complains about all sorts of things）.
• Intonation: When read aloud, there is usually a slight pause before/after each item, creating a rapid-fire listing feel that strengthens the complaining nuance.
meaning_vi: ～や・・・など、～とか・・・とか
Equivalent to the expression toka... toka
examples: 1. 私の部屋には漫画だの服だのが散らかっていて、寝る場所さえないほどだ。
My room is so cluttered with manga, clothes and so on that there isn't even room to sleep.
2. 彼女の話はいつも給料が少ないだの、仕事が忙しすぎるだの、文句ばかりだ。
All she ever talks about is how her pay is low, how her job is too busy and so on; it's nothing but complaints.
3. 彼はいつもスターになるだの映画を撮るだのと、夢のようなことばかり言っている。
He's always talking about dreamy things like becoming a star or making movies.
4. うちの親は毎日のように勉強しろだの、無駄づかいするなだの、うるさくて嫌になる。
Almost every day my parents nag me with "Study!", "Don't waste money!" and so on; it's so annoying I can't stand it.
mistakes: Wrong style: Using ～です／～ます before だの. Incorrect: 高いですだの安いですだの. Correct: 高いだの安いだの.
Giving only 1 item. Incorrect: 物価が高いだの. Correct: 物価が高いだの税金が上がるだの.
Using it in neutral formal documents. If you don't want a complaining nuance, switch to ～や～など or ～とか.
Misunderstanding it as a complete list like "and". In fact it means "for example…", with many other items implied.
Wrong word type: Forgetting "だ" with nouns/na-adjectives. Incorrect: 不便だの危険だの（ok because it is already na-adjective + だ? Note that だ is required）; with na-adjectives it must be 不便だだの危険だだの.
JLPT nuance trap: Sentences with ～だの are usually followed by verbs such as 言う／騒ぐ／して…, and the whole sentence has a complaining nuance. Choosing a neutral answer is wrong.
Logical order: The items should belong to the same category. Avoid combining items that are too far apart unless you intend to emphasize the messiness.
Punctuation: Separate long items with commas for readability: Aだの、Bだのと…

examples: Whether it's genuine or not, I'm not buying it.
Whether they are necessary or not, rules should be followed.
Whether the project is innovative or not, safety comes first.
Whether the price is high or not, we don't compromise on quality.
Whether he is a student or not, he cannot escape responsibility.
fields.explain:
The second clause expresses an unchanging position/condition:関係ない,影響されない,変わらない.
Firm, formal style; in spoken language it is often replaced by ～かどうかに関わらず or ～ても～なくても.
With N/ナ: であろうとなかろうと is preferred in argumentative writing.
Do not repeat the same phrase twice; state it once in the first clause, then give the conclusion.

～だろうとなかろうと expresses "whether or not it is/is said to be …", "regardless of whether … or not". It emphasizes that the decision/view in the second clause does not change, whatever the situation in the first clause.
• Stiff, rhetorical nuance; used to assert a position.
• "なかろう" is the archaic negative form of "ない" with the copula だ/である.
• Often used with contrasting pairs: 必要だろうとなかろうと, 重要だろうとなかろうと, 本物だろうとなかろうと.
• With i-adjectives: the "かろうとなかろうと" form is very written; in spoken language you can use "～くても～なくても".
fields.notes:
• With i-adjectives, "高かろうとなかろうと/多かろうとなかろうと/難しかろうとなかろうと" are patterns with a pleasing rhythm.
• "だろう" here is not real conjecture; it is a formal counterpart to "なかろう".
• In forceful statements, the structure can be repeated in parallel: Aだろうとなかろうと、Bであろうとなかろうと、結論…
mistakes: Applying it directly to verbs: "行くだろうとなかろうと" is unnatural; use "行こうが行くまいが/行くかどうかに関わらず".
Wrong i-adjective form: you must use "高かろうとなかろうと", not "高いだろうとなかろうと".
Mistaking だろう for conjecture: in this pattern it is a formal counterpart, not "probably".
JLPT: a trap is choosing ～ても～なくても; if the style is stiff and argumentative → choose ～であろうとなかろうと／～だろうとなかろうと.

rows: <ruby>本当<rt>ほんとう</rt></ruby>であろうとなかろうと
Whether one does it or not
<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>するかどうかに<ruby>関<rt>かか</rt></ruby>わらず
<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>でも<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>なくても

fields.connection: Vます + つ + Vます + つ (two opposite verbs)
examples: The staff member is going back and forth around the venue, checking the preparations.
I could see a small boat bobbing up and down on the waves.
The two engaged in a neck-and-neck race, overtaking and being overtaken.
The business talks went back and forth with pushing and pulling, and no agreement was reached.
I spent the whole day alternately reading and writing documents.
We have a relationship of give and take.
fields.explain:
Formal, written language; rare in everyday conversation except in fixed phrases.
Emphasizes balanced, prolonged repetition.
Usually comes before する or modifies a noun (～のN).
If you create your own verb pair, choose verbs with opposite meanings or two sides of the same activity.

The pattern ～つ～つ expresses two actions/states that alternate back and forth many times, creating a rhythmic, wave-like feel. Usually used in written language, with a literary/classical flavor.
• Focuses on the balanced alternation between the two parts (push-pull, go-return, float-sink...).
• Usually used with pairs of opposite or naturally corresponding verbs.
• Can describe both intentional actions and natural phenomena.
• Many cases are fixed phrases; the verbs cannot be swapped freely.
fields.notes:
• Phrases such as 持ちつ持たれつ and 抜きつ抜かれつ are very common in the press/sports.
• It can be followed by している／していた to indicate a continuing situation.
• Avoid attaching it to adjectives; this pattern is for verbs.
• Stylistic effect: creates rhythm and is rich in imagery. Suits explanatory and descriptive writing.
mistakes: Using the dictionary form instead of the continuative form (incorrect: 行くつ戻るつ → correct: 行きつ戻りつ).
Arbitrarily combining verbs that do not form a natural pair → sounds forced.
Using it in casual spoken language → unnatural (except in fixed phrases).
Confusing it with VてはV: both express repetition, but the nuance and form are different.

rows: Repeating over and over (doing, then doing again...)
More colloquial; no classical, rhythmic nuance
Lists two opposite actions that happen sometimes... sometimes...
Does not emphasize balanced alternation; neutral
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったり<ruby>戻<rt>もど</rt></ruby>ったりする
Uses the continuative form; usually a fixed phrase

examples: The construction work next door is unbearably noisy.
This room is unbearably hot and humid, isn't it?
I really can't handle crowds; I can't stand them.
I got bitten by mosquitoes, and the itching is unbearable.
I'm forced to listen to his bragging every day, and I can't stand it.
fields.explain:
A strong spoken complaint; avoid it in polite speech toward superiors unless adjusted: ～てかないません（rare, archaic). In practice かなわない is used.
The subject is the speaker or someone close whose feelings can be inferred; do not attribute it to others without signs of their feelings.
It is often accompanied by a clear cause, which makes the sentence more natural:風が強くてかなわない／匂いがきつくてかなわない.

• Expresses the speaker's feeling of "can't stand it/extremely unpleasant/bothersome" in response to some cause.
• Used only with a negative/complaining meaning. Stronger than ～てしょうがない/～てたまらない when complaining.
• Often used with adjectives such as うるさい／暑い／迷惑だ／不便だ／くさい…, or a specific cause: 人が多くてかなわない.
fields.notes:
• "かなわない" originally means "cannot match/cannot bear", and is usually written in kana.
• The form "～てはかなわない" is also found in written language: そんなことをされてはかなわない（it would be unbearable if that were done to me).
• Avoid using it with a positive sense: ×嬉しくてかなわない（use たまらない/しょうがない instead). meaning_vi: Cannot stand~ ⏐ explain: Limited to words that express emotions, sensations and desires.
Expresses the meaning of being unable to bear something, ~ very much. And it is often used for a bad impression. Adding は makes the sentence express a stronger degree of being unbearable. ⏐ examples: 1. 隣の工事がうるさくてかなわない。
The construction next door is so noisy that I can't stand it.
2. 私の家は、駅から遠くて不便でかなわない。
My house is far from the station, and it's terribly inconvenient.
mistakes: Using it with positive adjectives: ×楽しくてかなわない → wrong nuance.
Not stating a clear cause makes the sentence vague: add the agent/situation, e.g. "隣の犬が…"
Directly attributing someone else's feelings: ×彼は暑くてかなわないと思う → if guessing, add ようだ／らしい.

rows: Used with both positive and negative
～てしょうがない／～て<ruby>仕方<rt>しかた</rt></ruby>がない
More formal: しょうがない = <ruby>仕方<rt>しかた</rt></ruby>がない; a milder complaint than かなわない
Different meaning group; not a complaint
<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>むわけにはいかない

examples: My days are spent studying and then sleeping, sleeping and then studying.
My life goes on like this: exercising and then eating, eating and then exercising.
This room gets messy as soon as I clean it, and cluttered again as soon as I tidy it.
The weather kept raining and stopping, raining and stopping, for a whole week.
While I kept writing and erasing, erasing and writing, it had already become night.
Whenever I meet her, I always get nervous.
fields.explain:
Form: Verb in the te-form + は. Often preceded by a phrase marking the target/trigger with N＋に (彼女に会っては…).
Characteristics of the second clause: B is usually a psychological/emotional/reflexive response (緊張する・懐かしくなる・考え込む…). Avoid using B for a strongly intentional action.
Style: Natural in both spoken and written language when describing a habit; polite/gentle.
Timing: Often used when there are multiple observations in the past/present; not suited to a single event.

Meaning: Expresses the situation "whenever/every time A happens, B", where A is the trigger and B is a repeated reaction/result, usually an emotion or a natural state beyond one's control.

•
Repetition: Action/situation A repeats many times in reality; each repetition brings reaction B.

•
Nuance: Natural, habitual; often used for psychological states ("get nervous every time I meet", "get homesick every time I hear"). Different from the "alternating A then B" type, which is a symmetrical cycle.

•
Pragmatics: Used when the speaker wants to emphasize that the reaction certainly occurs every time there is a trigger.
fields.notes:
•
Scope of the subject: Usually the speaker/a person mentioned who has emotions; if the subject is a thing/nature, B should be a natural state (落ち着く・懐かしくなる… are also fine if the implied subject is a person).
•
Word combinations: Often used with verbs of perception/emotion: 見る・聞く・読む・会う・思い出す・緊張する・安心する・考え込む…
•
Emphatic nuance: 副詞 such as つい・いつも・決まって can be added to emphasize the regular repetition.
•
Turning it into a noun phrase: Use ～ては…ことがある/ことが多い to generalize a habit.
mistakes: Confusing it with "Vては〜V（alternation）": That pattern describes a symmetrical cycle (A then B, B then A). The present one is "every time A, B" and does not need a symmetrical part.
Choosing an unnatural second clause B: B should be a reaction/emotion or a result that follows; avoid strong commands/prohibitions.
Overusing it for a single event: ては implies repetition many times; using it for a single occurrence does not make sense.
Confusing it with "Vると": Vると emphasizes an inevitable rule, while ては leans toward a psychological habit each time a trigger occurs.

rows: Emphasizes trigger → repeated reaction. B is usually an emotion/natural state.
Every time A, B (neutral, broad meaning). Does not strongly suggest the psychological nuance of "being drawn into it" like ては.
Whenever A (an obvious condition), B (an inevitable result). Stronger sense of objective rule/cause and effect than ては.
たびに is purely "every time" and widely used; ては leans toward "every time… again" (a familiar emotion/response).
Different meaning: "A then B again, B then A again" (symmetrical/cyclical). Not trigger → reaction.

examples: He kept the shop going, even going into debt to do so.
He went to see her, even lying to his parents to do it.
I'll finish this project even if it means staying up all night.
I was moved by the sight of him saving people even at the risk of his own life.
I don't want to succeed if it means doing something like that.
fields.explain:
Usually used when stating a strong goal or criticizing excessive actions.
The preceding V is an "extreme" action (burdensome, sacrificial, unethical):嘘をつく,徹夜する,借金する,犯罪に手を染める…
The following part expresses a result/volition/evaluation: ～やる/～続ける/～行く/～価値はない.
Rarely used with trivial, ordinary actions; avoid using it with adjectives.
In rhetorical questions: そこまでする てまで ？ means "to that extent?".

• Expresses determination: "even if it means doing V (usually something excessive, undesirable or unreasonable), still …", "even going as far as V, …".
• Evaluative nuance: usually implies the judgment that this is an extreme, abnormal measure; it can be criticism (negative) or praise of determination (positive) depending on the context.
• The focus is the "limit point" まで: the speaker sets V as the maximum boundary that one still accepts crossing to reach the goal.
• ～てまでも emphasizes "even … ", and is more written than ～てまで. In spoken language, ～てまで is more common.
fields.notes:
• The pattern often appears in argumentative writing to criticize excessive trade-offs: 名誉を汚してまで…
• To praise a positive spirit of sacrifice, choose a verb with high value: 命をかけてまでも守る.
• Negative orientation: ～してまで…する価値はない states the view "it is not worth it".
mistakes: Using it with adjectives: incorrect. It must be a verb in the te-form.
Using it for small everyday things: unnatural. Reserve it for situations that "cross a limit".
Confusing it with ～ても: ～てまでも implies an extreme nuance and an evaluation; ～ても does not.
Getting the direction of meaning wrong: Vてまでも means "accepting doing V in order to …", not "because one did V, …".
In JLPT questions, the correct answer usually goes with verbs with a heavy nuance such as 嘘をつく, 犯罪に手を染める, 無理をする.

rows: Even if it means doing V (extreme), still …
<ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>をついてまでも<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>する。
Going as far as doing V, …
Spoken, more neutral; often used in critical sentences too.
<ruby>借金<rt>しゃっきん</rt></ruby>してまで<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>うなんて。
Uses a noun as the extreme measure.
<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>のコネまでして<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>る。
Does not imply "crossing a moral limit/difficulty".
Emphasizes determination; does not name a specific extreme action.
<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>が<ruby>何<rt>なん</rt></ruby>でも<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>する。
